questions.stem: A 51-year-old woman was found to have a raised serum creatinine of 2.5 mg/dL. She had undergone a kidney transplantation 9 months earlier. She was asymptomatic. Her immunosuppressive medications included tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone. She had normal renal function on previous follow-up visits and had a baseline creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL. No changes were made to her medications recently. Her urinalysis was normal.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: BK virus nephropathy BK virus nephropathy is asymptomatic and should be suspected when there is an unexplained rise in serum creatinine in kidney transplant recipients. The diagnosis is confirmed by the identification of decoy cells in urine cytology and detection of BK virus nucleic acid in urine and blood. Other options listed are typically symptomatic.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q40

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman presented with progressive headaches, confusion, and difficulty in walking. She was known to have relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis and had been treated with monthly natalizumab for 3 years. On examination she had bilateral lower extremity weakness. Sensation was intact. She had some word-finding difficulties. There was no photophobia or neck stiffness. Investigations: CT head: no mass effect seen. Asymmetric low attenuation foci in the periventricular and subcortical white matter.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Stop natalizumab and consider plasma exchange

questions.explanation: Stop natalizumab and consider plasma exchange Based on risk factors and clinical presentation, the diagnosis is most likely to be progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). The recommended treatment is to immediately stop the natalizumab, and some experts also recommend plasma exchange.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q37

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presented with fevers, dyspnea, cough, and an erythematous rash. He was day 115 after an HLAmismatched and T-cell-depleted allogeneic stem cell transplant for lymphoma. He had been treated at day 70 with prednisone for acute graft versus host disease. Investigations: Total white cell count 6.7 ×109/L CT chest: bilateral ground glass opacities BAL cultures and stains negative Urinalysis revealed hematuria with no bacteria on the stain Serum cytomegalovirus PCR undetectable
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Adenovirus The patient in this case is immunocompromised and at risk for many opportunistic infections, but the T-celldepleted graft and graft versus host disease are both risk factors for disseminated adenovirus infection. The hematuria in the case suggests adenovirus or BK virus, but BK virus would not cause the pneumonitis. HSV and VZV would be unusual causes of hematuria and diagnostic testing for CMV was negative.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q7

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man presented with a 6-week history of progressive right arm weakness and a 1-week history of increasing confusion and word-finding difficulties. He was known to have HIV , and although previously on ART he had been lost to clinical care and follow-up 3 years earlier. On physical exam, neurologic exam was notable for 3/5 strength in the right upper extremity and an expressive aphasia. Investigations: MRI of the brain: there are multiple discrete lesions in the cortical white matter and basal ganglia, which are hyperintense on the T2-weighted imaging sequences. CD4 count 125 cells/μL HIV viral load 45,200 copies/mL Serum RPR negative Serum cryptococcal antigen negative Toxoplasma IgG negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Antiretroviral therapy The most likely diagnosis given the clinical syndrome and characteristic findings on MRI of the brain is progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) caused by JC virus. The recommended treatment for PML is immediate initiation of ART to achieve immune reconstitution. Treatments such as cidofovir, cytarabine, and 5HT2a serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as mirtazapine have been tested but have shown no or inconclusive clinical benefit. The antivirals aciclovir and ganciclovir do not have activity against JC virus.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q22

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man with polycystic kidney disease underwent cadaveric renal transplantation, cytomegalovirus D/R-, HLA-incompatible. His immunosuppressive regimen consisted of tacrolimus, prednisolone, and mycophenolate mofetil. He was taking trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole for PCP prophylaxis. At 10 months after the transplantation he reported rose-colored urine. He was otherwise well. Urinalysis: leukocytes ++, hematuria +++ Creatinine 238 μmol/L
questions.lead_in: What investigation is most likely to be diagnostic?
questions.explanation: Renal biopsy This is a case of BK virus nephropathy. The definitive diagnosis of BKVN requires a renal biopsy showing polyomavirus-induced cytopathic changes in tubular or glomerular epithelial cells.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q46

questions.question: BK nephropathy laboratory evaluation.

parts.text: Name three laboratory tests that can be used to evaluate for BK nephropathy.

parts_raw.text: Name three laboratory tests that can be used to evaluate for BK nephropathy.

questions.model_answer: (1) Urine testing: BKV DNA PCR (viruria almost always precedes viremia) and/or urine cytology for decoy cells (enlarged nucleus with single large basophilic intranuclear inclusion). (2) Plasma BKV DNA quantitative PCR (NPV 100%; plasma viral load >10^4 copies/mL predicts histologic nephropathy). (3) Renal biopsy (essential/gold standard): tubular epithelial viral inclusions with cell detachment, SV40 immunostain positive.

questions.question: What are 4 neurological manifestations of JC virus?

parts.text: What are 4 neurological manifestations of JC virus?

parts_raw.text: What are 4 neurological manifestations of JC virus?

questions.model_answer: (1) Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) - coordination difficulty, gait imbalance, cognitive dysfunction, visual problems, limb paresis. (2) JCV granule cell neuronopathy - cerebellar atrophy, gait ataxia, incoordination. (3) JCV encephalopathy - global cognitive decline and aphasia from cortical pyramidal neuron infection. (4) JCV meningitis - headache, neck stiffness, diplopia.

cohort_answer.text: PML (progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy); Cognitive/behavioural changes (36-54%); Motor/hemiparesis (33-45%); Gait incoordination/ataxia (35%); Visual changes (19-41%); Speech/language (24-40%)

questions.question: A 50-year-old man with HIV, CD4 count 50 cells/uL, non-adherent to antiretroviral therapy, presents with ataxia and vague neurologic symptoms and no headache. No focal deficits on examination. No travel history; lives in Toronto. No lumbar puncture performed. MRI brain shows diffuse multifocal lesions.
questions.question_raw: 50yo M HIV positive patient with CD4 count 50copies/mL, non-compliant with ART presenting with ataxia and vague neuro symptoms, no headaches. No focal neuro symptoms on exam. No history of travel, lives in Toronto. No LP given. MRI brain shows diffuse multifocal lesions.

parts.text: Give four pathogens and their associated syndromes to explain the clinical presentation.

parts_raw.text: Give 4 pathogens and their associated syndromes to explain the clinical presentation.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) JC polyomavirus - progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy: multifocal non-enhancing white-matter lesions without mass effect, ataxia, hemiparesis, visual and cognitive decline. (2) HIV-1 itself - HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder/HIV encephalopathy: symmetric periventricular white-matter change with atrophy, psychomotor slowing, gait instability. (3) Cytomegalovirus - CMV encephalitis/ventriculoencephalitis (also polyradiculomyelitis): periventricular enhancement, confusion, cranial neuropathies at CD4 <50. (4) Mycobacterium tuberculosis - tuberculous meningitis with basal meningeal enhancement, tuberculomas and infarcts. (Also consider Toxoplasma gondii encephalitis and primary CNS lymphoma, though both typically show ring enhancement and mass effect.)

questions.question: BK nephropathy - what are 3 modes of laboratory tests to do for diagnosis?
questions.question_raw: AM 8. BK nephropathy - What are 3 modes of laboratory tests to do for diagnosis? (1.5)

parts.text: What are 3 modes of laboratory tests to do for diagnosis?

parts_raw.text: What are 3 modes of laboratory tests to do for diagnosis?

questions.model_answer: (1) Urine BKV DNA PCR (viruria) and/or urine cytology showing decoy cells. (2) Plasma BKV DNA quantitative PCR (NPV 100%; load >10^4 copies/mL sensitive/specific for histologic nephropathy). (3) Renal biopsy with SV40 immunostain (tubular viral inclusions; ~30% false-negative from focal disease).

cohort_answer.text: DNA NAT (urine - highly sensitive, less specific, look for viral loads >2.5x10^7; serum - highly specific to trigger biopsy if >4 log or change in meds); Urine cytology (decoy cells, classic for polyomavirus); Histopathology (gold standard - renal biopsy with IF stain SV40). Algorithm: Urine NAT -> Serum NAT -> Histopathology (serology not useful for diagnosis).

questions.question: A man with HIV who has lived in Toronto his entire life is non-adherent to antiretroviral therapy with a CD4 count of 50 cells/uL. He presents with three weeks of altered level of consciousness and ataxia. MRI shows scattered white matter lesions without mass effect.
questions.question_raw: Gentleman with HIV has lived in Toronto his entire life. Noncompliant with ART and CD4 is 50. Presents with 3 weeks of altered LOC and ataxia. MRI shows scattered white matter lesions without mass effect.

parts.text: What are the four most likely organisms and the diseases they cause?

parts_raw.text: What are the 4 most likely organisms and diseases they cause?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) JC polyomavirus - progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (asymmetric, non-enhancing white-matter lesions, no mass effect; diagnosis by CSF JC virus PCR). (2) HIV-1 - HIV encephalopathy/HIV-associated dementia with diffuse symmetric white-matter signal change and atrophy. (3) Cytomegalovirus - CMV encephalitis/ventriculoencephalitis at CD4 <50. (4) Mycobacterium tuberculosis - tuberculous meningoencephalitis with basal meningitis and infarction. Cryptococcus neoformans meningoencephalitis is the other key consideration; Toxoplasma encephalitis and primary CNS lymphoma are less likely given the absence of mass effect.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort lists HSV and VZV as leading answers; in advanced HIV with subacute multifocal white-matter disease and no mass effect, PML, HIV encephalopathy, CMV and tuberculosis are the higher-yield answers.

cohort_answer.text: PML - JC Virus; CMV; HSV; VZV; TB (possible to get hydrocephalus though). Other differentials more likely to have mass effect/increased ICP: Toxoplasmosis, Cryptococcal. Non-infectious ddx: CNS lymphoma (causes mass effect).

questions.model_answer: (1) Plasma/blood BKV DNA quantitative PCR (NPV 100%; used to rule out nephropathy and trigger biopsy). (2) Urine BKV DNA PCR (viruria; sustained viruria 100% sensitive, 94% specific for viremia). (3) Urine cytology for decoy cells (enlarged nucleus with single large basophilic intranuclear inclusion).

cohort_answer.text: Quantitative PCR in plasma (100% sens, 88% spec); quantitative PCR in urine (100% sens, 78% spec); urine cytology - infected "decoy" cells with large nuclei and single large basophilic intranuclear inclusion (sens 25%, spec 84%); histopathology - kidney biopsy with Haufen (characteristic but not specific).

parts_raw.text: What are 4 risk factors for BK virus hemorrhagic cystitis in allogeneic stem cell transplant?
What urine based test other than blood can be used for diagnosis?
What are 2 antivirals from different classes that can be used for treatment?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Myeloablative conditioning regimen. (2) Graft-versus-host disease (immune reconstitution). (3) Allogeneic (vs autologous) graft. (4) HLA-mismatched/unrelated donor graft (also BKV seropositivity, older age). b) Urine BKV DNA PCR (viruria); urine cytology for decoy cells is an adjunct. c) Intravesical/IV cidofovir (nucleotide analog) and a fluoroquinolone - ciprofloxacin (inhibits BKV-encoded DNA gyrase; prophylaxis reduces post-HSCT hemorrhagic cystitis).
questions.beyond_mandell: Naming ciprofloxacin/cidofovir as being from different drug classes reflects standard classification; the chapter presents both agents but does not frame them as a two-drug regimen.

questions.question: A patient with autologous stem cell transplant develops BK virus hemorrhagic cystitis.
questions.question_raw: Q72 2023 Day 1. AutoSCT with BK hemorrhagic cystitis. (VIRUSES)

parts.text: Four risk factors.
One urinary test to diagnose, in addition to her symptoms.
Which 2 antiviral drugs to treat.

parts_raw.text: 4 risk factors
One urinary test to diagnose, in addition to her symptoms
Which 2 antiviral drugs to treat

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Myeloablative conditioning regimen. (2) Graft-versus-host disease. (3) Allogeneic graft (hemorrhagic cystitis rarely seen in autologous recipients). (4) HLA-mismatched/unrelated donor graft (also BKV seropositivity, older age). b) Urine BKV DNA PCR (viruria) - increased urine viral load with hematuria supports the diagnosis. c) Cidofovir (intravesical or IV) and ciprofloxacin (fluoroquinolone).
questions.beyond_mandell: The chapter notes BKV hemorrhagic cystitis is characteristically an allogeneic (not autologous) HSCT complication; treatment evidence for cidofovir/ciprofloxacin is limited to case series and small retrospective studies.

cohort_answer.text:
4 risk factors: Myeloablative conditioning regimens (HLA mismatch higher risk); haploidentical donor; GVHD (acute and chronic); CMV reactivation; male sex.
Urinary test/symptoms: Typically BK viruria; BKPyV serum can help with diagnosis; BK viremia >10,000 copies/mL more likely to occur; symptoms - cystitis (dysuria, urgency, abdominal pain), hematuria, AKI.
2 antiviral drugs: Intravesicular and IV Cidofovir (no RCT data, some observational studies); Brincidofovir (pro-drug of Cidofovir); Leflunomide (has some antiviral properties against BKV).

questions.question: Polyomaviruses.

parts.text: What are two viruses from the polyomavirus family and what is the MOST common clinical syndrome?
Fill in the blanks: polyomavirus is a ______ (RNA or DNA) virus and has ______ (an envelope or no envelope).
How do you manage polyomavirus infection in someone with HIV/AIDS.

parts_raw.text: What are two viruses from the polyomavirus family and what is the MOST common clinic syndrome?
Fill in the blanks, polyomavirus is an ______ (RNA or DNA) virus and has ______ (an envelop or no envelope)
How do you manage polyomavirus infection in someone with HIV/AIDS.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) BK virus - most common syndrome is BKV-associated nephropathy in renal transplant recipients (and hemorrhagic cystitis in HSCT). (2) JC virus - most common syndrome is progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. b) DNA virus; no envelope (non-enveloped). c) The mainstay is immune restoration: initiate or optimize antiretroviral therapy to reconstitute JCV-specific cellular immunity (raises PML 1-year survival from 10% to 50%); no specific antiviral is proven. In inflammatory PML-IRIS with mass effect, a short course of corticosteroids may be used sparingly.
questions.beyond_mandell: The DNA/non-enveloped structure of polyomaviruses (part b) is established virology not stated in this chapter slice.

questions.question: What are 4 neurological manifestations of JC virus?
questions.question_raw: 24. What are 4 neurological manifestations of JC virus? (4)

parts.text: What are 4 neurological manifestations of JC virus?

parts_raw.text: What are 4 neurological manifestations of JC virus? (4)

questions.model_answer: (1) Classic progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) - lytic infection of oligodendrocytes/astrocytes causing multifocal white matter demyelination and focal deficits based on lesion location. (2) PML-immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (PML-IRIS) - inflammatory PML on immune recovery (e.g. ART), with contrast-enhancing lesions and worsening symptoms. (3) JCV granule cell neuronopathy (GCN) - infection/destruction of cerebellar granule cell neurons causing cerebellar atrophy, gait ataxia and incoordination without demyelination. (4) JCV encephalopathy - infection of hemispheric cortical pyramidal neurons with global cognitive decline and aphasia (JCV meningitis is an additional recognized syndrome).

cohort_answer.text: PML (progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy) - Classic (no edema around lesions on MRI) or IRIS (edema around lesions on MRI). JC virus granule cell neuronopathy - focus of infection in cerebellum with destruction of granule cells, diagnosed on cerebellar biopsy or PCR. JC virus meningitis. JC virus encephalitis/encephalopathy - gray matter infection.

questions.question: A patient presents with subacute neurologic deficits in the setting of immunosuppression or immunomodulatory therapy, with brain MRI showing focal or multifocal white matter lesions without mass effect that do not conform to vascular territories, suggestive of PML. How do you diagnose it?
questions.question_raw: Clinical scenario suggestive of PML. "The diagnosis of PML should be suspected in patients who present with subacute neurologic deficits in the setting of immunosuppression or immunomodulatory therapy if brain MRI reveals focal or multifocal white matter lesions, generally without mass effect, that do not conform to vascular territories."

parts.text: How do you diagnose it?

parts_raw.text: How do you dx?

questions.model_answer: Diagnosis follows a histopathologic or a clinical/radiologic pathway. (1) MRI (imaging of choice, more sensitive than CT): multiple subcortical white matter lesions sparing cortex, not conforming to vascular territories, hyperintense on T2/FLAIR and hypointense on T1, generally without mass effect or enhancement. (2) CSF: nonspecific profile (mild pleocytosis, mildly elevated protein, normal glucose) plus JCV DNA by PCR - sensitivity 72-92% and specificity 92-100% (PCR sensitivity falls to ~58% in the post-ART era on ART). (3) Brain biopsy is the gold standard (sensitivity 64-96%, specificity 100%): demyelination, reactive gliosis, enlarged bizarre astrocytes, myelin-laden macrophages, and JCV in oligodendrocytes with enlarged amphophilic nuclei. Clinical diagnosis rests on compatible clinical/radiologic findings not better explained otherwise plus JCV PCR in CSF (classified certain, probable, possible, or not PML).

cohort_answer.text: MRI with and without GAD – lesions typically white matter sparing cortex but do not conform to vascular territory. CSF: mild pleocytosis, slightly elevated protein, normal glucose. PCR 72-92% sensitive, 92-100% specific. Brain Bx (Gold standard): demyelination, bizarre astrocytes, enlarged oligodendroglial nuclei

questions.question: A patient presents with a clinical scenario suggestive of PML. What is the cause?

parts.text: What is the cause?

parts_raw.text: Cause?

questions.model_answer: PML is caused by the human polyomavirus JC virus (JCV). Primary infection occurs in childhood and is asymptomatic, after which the virus becomes clinically latent (kidney, lymphoid tissue, and probably bone marrow/brain). In profound cellular immunosuppression JCV reactivates and productively infects oligodendrocytes and astrocytes in the brain, causing lytic infection and demyelination.

cohort_answer.text: PML caused by reactivation of the polyomavirus JC (JCV). Asymptomatic primary infection occurs in childhood, antibodies found in 86% of adults. JCV remains latent in kidneys and lymphoid organs, but in profound cellular immunosuppression can reactivate

questions.question: A patient presents with a clinical scenario suggestive of PML. Outline treatment, management, and workup.

parts.text: Outline treatment, management, and workup.

parts_raw.text: Treatment/Management/Workup

questions.model_answer: Workup: clinical/neurologic exam, MRI with and without gadolinium, CSF for JCV DNA PCR (mild pleocytosis, elevated protein, normal glucose), and brain biopsy if diagnosis remains uncertain. Treatment: no specific antiviral therapy exists. The mainstay is restoration of immunity - in HIV-positive patients, initiate/optimize ART (raises 1-year survival from ~10% to 50%); in HIV-negative patients, reduce/withdraw immunosuppression to allow adaptive immune control. Trials of cidofovir, cytarabine, mefloquine, and mirtazapine have not shown consistent benefit. In inflammatory PML/PML-IRIS with brain swelling and mass effect, a short course of corticosteroids may be used sparingly for life-threatening edema/impending herniation.

cohort_answer.text: Treatment: immune reconstitution – if HIV+, start ARV; if not HIV+, consider reducing immunosuppression. No antivirals. Workup: Clinical exam, MRI, CSF for JCV PCR, +/- brain bx

questions.question: What are 3 ways (specifically microbiological tests) to assess for BK virus in a renal transplant patient?

parts.text: What are 3 ways (specifically microbiological tests) to assess for BK virus in a renal transplant patient?

parts_raw.text: What are 3-ways to assess for BK virus in a renal transplant patient (specifically microbiological test)

questions.model_answer: (1) Plasma/blood BKV DNA PCR (quantitative) - screened at regular intervals post-transplant; NPV ~100% but PPV only ~50% for nephropathy, though a plasma viral load above 10,000 copies/mL has ~93% sensitivity and specificity for histologic nephropathy. (2) Urine BKV DNA PCR - viruria almost always precedes viremia; sustained viruria (two or more consecutive samples) is ~100% sensitive and ~94% specific for BK viremia. (3) Urine cytology for decoy cells - enlarged nuclei with a single large basophilic intranuclear inclusion indicating viral infection (not specific to BKV; also seen with CMV/adenovirus).

cohort_answer.text: BK virus blood qPCR - regular intervals following transplant; BKVL > 10,000 copies/mL -> moderate PPV for rejection from BKVAN. Urine microscopy to look for 'decoy cells'. Urine BK PCR. Urine Haufen - requires electron microscopy, not widely available
